article_content: The house of the future might be built from lightweight bioplastic and resemble a spiderâs web â if the London-based architecture collective Softkill Design has its way. The group has designed what they claim could be the worldâs first fully 3D-printed home, with a prototype potentially ready for assembly by summer 2013. Unlike conventional construction, this home wouldnât use bricks, mortar, or steel. Instead, its components â each just 0.7 millimetres thick â would be manufactured off-site using laser-sintered bioplastic, then assembled on location in a single day using Velcro or button-like fasteners. This design, called Protohouse 2.0, builds on an earlier prototype unveiled at the 3D Print Show in London in October 2012. That initial model featured a fibrous nylon structure inspired by bone architecture. Protohouse 2.0 refines the concept, using minimal material to maximize structural integrity. Gilles Retsin, a member of Softkill Design, explained to Dezeen.com that printing with sand or concrete on-site lacks the precision needed for such delicate structures. âIn a factory setting, we can use stronger materials like plastics or metals,â he said. Retsin also dismissed a rival project by Dutch firm Universe Architecture, noting that it only 3D-prints formwork before filling it with concrete â meaning the final structure isnât truly printed. âThatâs not 3D printing the building,â he argued. While costs havenât been disclosed, Retsin believes economies of scale in the growing 3D printing industry could make these homes economically viable in the near future â offering a potential solution to housing shortages.

article_content: Love and empathy are often celebrated as hallmarks of human kindness â yet new research suggests they can sometimes fuel surprising forms of aggression. Scientists at the University at Buffalo have found that feelings of deep compassion, far from always promoting peace, can lead people to act aggressively â not out of anger, but out of devotion. The key lies in two neurohormones: oxytocin and vasopressin. These chemicals, produced by nerve cells, donât just make us feel warm and fuzzy; they also push us to act â even if that means harming someone else to help a loved one. According to lead researcher Michael Poulin, this isnât about personal grievance or self-defense. Itâs about loyalty. When we see someone we care about being threatened, our brains may trigger an instinct to remove the obstacle â even if that obstacle is innocent. Think of a parent sabotaging their childâs rival in a school contest, or a soldier risking everything to shield a fellow soldier, even if it means hurting an enemy who hasnât directly harmed them. This phenomenon was explored through both surveys and lab experiments. In one study, participants read a story about a stranger forced to eat hot sauce for a pain experiment. Those with higher levels of oxytocin and vasopressin were more likely to choose to inflict greater pain on a competitor â someone standing in the way of the strangerâs relief. In another, people recalled times someone close to them was mistreated; those who felt strong compassion were more likely to describe wanting to hurt the perpetrator â even if the perpetrator hadn't broken any rules. Interestingly, earlier research from the University of California found that atheists and agnostics were more likely than devoutly religious people to act generously based purely on emotional compassion â not religious duty. Their giving came from the heart, not the doctrine. Together, these findings suggest compassion doesnât always mean gentleness. Sometimes, it means choosing sides â even at the cost of fairness.

article_content: On Thursday, the Kerala-based CSIR-National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology (CSIR-NIIST) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), Bengaluru, to collaborate on advancing Indiaâs aerospace and defence sectors. The MoU, signed and exchanged in Bengaluru, focuses on the development of magnesium and aluminium alloy castings, along with related technologies for aerospace and defence applications. Senior scientists and officials from both organisations witnessed the signing ceremony. The agreement enables CSIR-NIIST to collaborate with HAL on human resource sharing, facility utilisation, technology support, consultancy, and joint research in the field of light alloys for designing and developing aerospace components and welding solutions. Key collaboration areas include manufacturing aeronautical-grade magnesium alloy castings using the low-pressure casting (LPC) process, designing filler materials for salvage welding of aluminium and magnesium castings, and pursuing other mutually beneficial research domains. A constituent laboratory of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), CSIR-NIIST Trivandrum is a leading institution conducting advanced R&D in resource utilisation critical to national development. HAL designs, develops, manufactures, supplies, and maintains aircraft, helicopters, aerospace systems, and components.

article_content: A pensioner who killed her husband of 50 years after he was diagnosed with terminal leukemia has claimed the act was one of mercy. At Luton Crown Court, Sheila Sampford pleaded guilty to strangling her 82-year-old husband, John Sampford, who was dying of leukemia at their home in Milton Keynes, Buckinghamshire. She insisted her motive was to end his suffering and now faces a separate hearing to determine whether the killing constituted a mercy killing. Mr. Sampford was found dead on July 5 last year. His wife was arrested the same day and initially told police his death resulted from a suicide pact. Sampford appeared via video link from Peterborough Prison, where she is held on remand. After entering her guilty plea, the judge ordered a further hearing to establish the facts before sentencing. Prosecutor Neil Moore stated: 'The central issue is whether she believed this killing was an act of mercy.' Defense counsel John Price QC added: 'The only question is whether he asked her to do what she did.' Euthanasia â derived from the Greek for 'good death' â refers to a patient consenting to have another person, typically a doctor, end their life. While legal in some European countries and U.S. states, both euthanasia and assisted suicide remain criminal offenses in the UK. Judge Richard Foster ordered a separate hearing to clarify the circumstances before determining sentence. Although murder carries an automatic life sentence, a finding of mercy may influence the minimum term before parole eligibility.

article_content: A groundbreaking study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences challenges the traditional way scientists measure impactâby simply counting citations. Researchers led by Alex Gates from the University of Virginiaâs School of Data Science argue that citation numbers often misrepresent real influence because theyâre skewed by differences in how fields publish and cite work over time. To fix this, Gates and his colleaguesâQing Ke from City University of Hong Kong and Albert-LÃ¡szlÃ³ BarabÃ¡si from Northeastern Universityâhave developed a smarter system. Instead of raw counts, their method adjusts citation data using a network model that accounts for discipline norms and historical trends. This allows for a fairer comparison of breakthroughs across physics, biology, computer science, or even decades apart. Whatâs more, the team didnât just publish theoryâthey built a free, open-source tool so any researcher can test it on their own work. Gates, who joined UVA in 2022, says this could help level the playing field for interdisciplinary science and give under-cited but high-impact papers a fair shot at recognition.

article_content: Starting in September 2015, Englandâs A-levels are undergoing a major overhaul to bring back academic depth and reduce reliance on coursework. The goal? To make these exams tougher, fairer, and better aligned with university expectations. In English literature, students will now study at least eight texts â down from twelve â with strict requirements: one must be a Shakespeare play, at least three must come from before 1900, and one must be written after 2000. This shift encourages students to engage deeply with literary evolution across centuries. Theyâll also face an unseen text in their exams, pushing them to develop broader reading habits and sharper analytical skills. History students will explore events spanning at least 200 years instead of the previous 100-year window, and the proportion of British-focused content will drop from 25% to 20%, assuming students already have a solid foundation from GCSE. Meanwhile, maths-heavy concepts are being woven into biology, chemistry, physics, economics, computer science, and psychology exams to reflect the growing quantitative demands of modern disciplines. Coursework, once a staple, is being phased out except where hands-on skills are essential â like geography fieldwork or art practicals. AS-levels are no longer part of the A-level grade; theyâre now standalone certificates. These reforms, shaped by a review led by Lancaster Universityâs Professor Mark Smith, aim to stop schools from teaching to short-term exams and instead foster long-term intellectual growth.

article_content: In an era where most electronics are built to break and be replaced, a quiet revolution is brewing â one where people are turning back to handcrafting, customizing, and building things with their own hands. At the heart of this shift is Dominic Muren, a Seattle-based innovator who founded The Humblefactory to give makers the tools they need to create what big companies wonât â or canât â produce. One such invention? The Egg-Bot â a quirky little machine that turns ordinary eggs into canvases for intricate drawings. Another? The DODOcase â a beautifully crafted tablet cover modeled after classic book bindings. What makes these more than novelties is their impact: the DODOcase didnât just sell well â it rescued a century-old bookbinding workshop in San Francisco, bringing back 10 jobs during the worst of the recession. Muren doesnât see this as just about products. He sees it as a cultural awakening. Inspired by publications like 'Make' magazine and the book 'Makers,' a growing community of tinkerers, artists, and engineers are rejecting mass-produced sameness. Theyâre crafting items that reflect personal taste, not marketing trends. And hereâs the twist: while many in the U.S. and Europe treat 'making' as a new trend, Muren points out that much of the rest of the world never stopped. 'We call it a movement,' he says, 'but in many cultures, making has always been part of daily life.' That convergence â between rediscovery and enduring tradition â is what excites him most. At events like PopTech, Muren highlights these creations not as gimmicks, but as symbols of deeper change: the joy of turning imagination into reality. 'The real magic,' he says, 'isnât in the egg or the case â itâs in realizing that the gap between nothing and something? That was me.'

article_content: On a busy morning in central London, more than 900 people were safely evacuated from The Shard â Europeâs tallest building â after emergency crews responded to reports of thick smoke rising from its basement. Though no fire was confirmed, the London Fire Brigade deployed seven engines and approximately 50 firefighters to investigate. Crews lifted street manhole covers and inspected nearby infrastructure, including a power substation operated by UK Power Networks, which was temporarily accessed by technicians to rule out an electrical fault. The operation lasted roughly three hours, with the safety perimeter cleared just before 2 p.m. Officials repeatedly emphasized there was no evidence of an actual blaze, and no injuries were reported. Despite this, the incident triggered significant disruption, particularly for guests staying at the upscale Shangri-La Hotel located inside the tower. Many were left waiting outdoors on the chilly plaza with little assistance, fueling complaints about poor crisis communication. Rumors quickly circulated that a senior member of Qatarâs royal family â one of the buildingâs owners â had been inside and evacuated. However, spokespersons for The Shard firmly denied any members of the royal family were present. The event, while ultimately a false alarm, became an unexpected PR challenge for the luxury hotel, whose high-end clientele experienced the chaos firsthand. The Shard, completed in 2012 and standing at 306 meters, remains a landmark symbol of Londonâs skyline â and a reminder that even the most secure buildings can trigger widespread concern over something as simple as smoke.

article_content: Kool & The Gang drummer and founding member George 'Funky' Brown has died, his family announced on Friday. He was 74. 'We lost our beloved husband and father, Kool & The Gang founding member George Brown, last night,' read a statement provided by the family to ABC Audio. 'He passed away peacefully at Long Beach Memorial Hospital, surrounded by family. His incredible talent and presence will be greatly missed and never forgotten.' Kool & The Gang also paid tribute to Brown on Facebook, calling him 'the funkiest drummer the world has ever seen.' They added, 'His beautiful soul is now at rest. We love you, George. Thank you for giving us the sound of happiness.' Brown co-founded Kool & The Gang in New Jersey in 1974 alongside brothers Robert 'Kool' Bell and Ronald Bell, Dennis 'Dee Tee' Thomas, Robert 'Spike' Mickens, Charles Smith, Woodrow 'Woody' Sparrow, and Claydes Smith. In addition to playing drums, Brown co-wrote many of the group's biggest hits, including their No. 1 classic 'Celebration,' as well as 'Ladies Night,' 'Jungle Boogie,' 'Get Down On It,' and 'Too Hot.' Brown, the Bell brothers, and Claydes Smith were inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2018, and the group was inducted into the New Jersey Hall of Fame in 2015. Although the lineup of Kool & The Gang has changed over the years, Brown remained a performing member until his death and was one of the longest-serving members alongside Robert 'Kool' Bell. Bell is now the last surviving founding member of the group.

article_content: Sir James Munby, President of the Family Division, said he will consult lawyers, judges, and social work leaders on the possibility of allowing public attendance in certain types of family court cases. For the first time, members of the public may be permitted to observe proceedings involving children taken into state care, adoption disputes, and residency decisions following family breakdowns. In the past, these cases have been held in private due to concerns that neighbors or acquaintances might attend court and spread harmful rumors about the children involved. Sir James plans to release a paper soon outlining proposals to end secrecy in family and Court of Protection courts, including preliminary consultation views. The Daily Mailâs campaign against secret justice has drawn attention to controversial rulings made behind closed doors â including the 2022 revelation that the Court of Protection secretly detained 50-year-old Wanda Maddocks for attempting to remove her elderly father from a care home she believed endangered him. Since then, Sir James has banned secret detentions and mandated that judges publish their rulings in both family and Court of Protection cases. While approved journalists have been allowed in family courts since 2009 under a policy introduced by then-Labour Justice Secretary Jack Straw, the rules applied only to reporters and permitted judges to impose reporting restrictions preventing any details from being published. Sir Jamesâs upcoming consultation will also advocate for releasing court documents so observers can understand legal arguments based on previously confidential materials, and for clearer advance notice of scheduled cases. 'I will be canvassing views on how this guidance can be improved â and possibly expanded,' Sir James said in a circular to judges.

article_content: In early September, my iPhone 5 slipped off the roof of my Jetta wagon while I was driving on the highway. At the local Apple Store, I was given two choices: repair the cracked screen for $149âor swap it for a brand-new iPhone 5 for $229. But since my phone was nearly a year old, I wasnât eligible to upgrade to the then-unannounced iPhone 5s, I didnât have AppleCare, and I figured the fresh battery in a new unit made the $229 price feel like a deal. So I swapped it. This experience highlights how Apple has long offered in-store repairsâand now, it appears theyâre dramatically expanding the program. For example, technicians will soon be able to replace and recalibrate touchscreens on the iPhone 5s and 5câfor the same $149 price. Other components expected to be repairable in-store include volume buttons, the vibration motor, rear camera, speaker system, and the Home button (though not the Touch ID-enabled version on the iPhone 5s). If you have AppleCare, these repairs are free. Without it, expect to pay $79 for a new battery and $29 for a Home button replacement. article_content: A recent report by the Office for National Statistics reveals a sharp rise in the number of British households containing five or more peopleâa trend largely driven by whatâs being called the 'sandwich generation.' These are adults juggling responsibilities for both their children and aging parents, often under one roof. Economic pressures, especially the soaring cost of housing, mean many young adults canât afford to move out. In fact, over half a million homes in England and Wales now house six or more people, marking a 25% spike over the past decade. This growth has been observed across nearly all regions, except the North East. Areas like Newham in East London, along with Luton, Slough, Bradford, Birmingham, and Leicester, have the highest concentrations of such large households. The ONS notes that these areas also tend to have larger populations from South Asian backgrounds, where multigenerational living is culturally common. Meanwhile, traditional nuclear families with children are becoming less common, dropping from 43% to 41% of all households in ten years. In 2013, nearly 3.3 million Britons aged 20 to 34 were still living with their parentsâup 25% since 1996. Among 20- to 24-year-olds, almost half lived at home; by age 30, that number dropped sharply, and by 34, only about 8% of men and 3% of women remained in parental homes. Experts point to two main reasons: income tends to rise through a personâs twenties before plateauing, and the likelihood of forming a partnership increases with age, prompting independent living.

His fellow activist Ilya Yashin explained the symbolism: 'Putin isnât just a leader â heâs the architect of the system that crushed political competition.' Though Putinâs approval ratings had dipped, polls still predicted a comfortable win in the upcoming March election. Still, protesters refused to back down. They began experimenting with creative acts of defiance â from coffee art featuring Putinâs face to cars adorned with white ribbons and balloons circling Moscowâs Garden Ring. Putin dismissed the demonstrations as orchestrated by Western agents, yet the movementâs persistence signaled a shift. As Yelizarov noted, 'Theyâre not listening. So weâre finding new ways to be heard.' The banner may have been removed, but its message echoed far beyond the river.

article_content: The human body, with 100 billion neurons and 37 trillion cells, is far too complex for current computers to artificially replicate. But what if scientists started smaller? A team behind the OpenWorm project has done exactly thatâcreating a digital and physical replica of Caenorhabditis elegans, one of the simplest known multicellular organisms. C. elegans is a transparent, 1-millimeter-long nematode with 302 neurons and 959 cells. Despite its simplicity, it exhibits behaviors like finding mates and avoiding threats. It was the first multicellular organism to have its entire genome mappedâand shares about 80% of its genes with humans, making it a vital model for biological research. The OpenWorm initiative, involving researchers across the U.S. and U.K., has digitally reconstructed every neuron and cell of C. elegans, simulating how they fire and interact. This digital 'brain' has been implanted into a Lego Mindstorms EV3 robot, enabling it to move, turn, and navigate obstacles like a living worm. The robot currently lacks complex functions like feeding, but it represents a major milestone in bio-inspired robotics. The ultimate goal is to release 'WormSim'âa downloadable simulationâfor public education and research by next year, following a successful Kickstarter campaign. While the project focuses on modeling life at its most basic level, it raises broader questions about artificial intelligence. Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, has warned that unchecked AI development could lead to dangerous outcomes within five years, citing risks from digital superintelligences and autonomous bots. Though unrelated to OpenWorm, his comments underscore the ethical urgency surrounding synthetic life systems.

article_content: Researchers at Duke University may have uncovered the molecular trigger behind the painful, itchy sensation of sunburn. The culprit? A protein called TRPV4, found abundantly in the skinâs outer layer. In experiments with mice and human tissue, scientists observed that those lacking TRPV4 showed minimal damage after UVB exposureâunlike typical mice, whose skin blistered and became hypersensitive. An experimental blocker applied to the skin replicated this protective effect. Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the findings suggest future sunscreens could incorporate TRPV4 inhibitors to enhance protection beyond traditional UV filters. While experts applaud the potential to reduce skin cancer ratesâespecially critical as it's the most common cancer in the UK and rising sharply among youthâthey stress the need for more research. Dr. Wolfgang Liedtke, a senior author, warns that inhibiting TRPV4 might affect other skin functions, suggesting it may best be combined with existing sunblocks. Interestingly, the team also sees broader implications: understanding sunburn pain could unlock new ways to treat chronic pain conditions, such as those experienced by accident survivors. Dermatologist Matt Gass called the discovery 'very interesting,' noting its possible 'profound impact' on public health if validated through further studies.

article_content: Staying physically active may help shield the brain from Alzheimerâs â even for people who carry a gene that greatly increases their risk. A long-term study involving adults aged 60 to 80 found that those who exercised at least three times a week maintained healthier brain volume, especially in the hippocampus, the region tied to memory. This protective effect held true even among individuals carrying the APOE-e4 gene, which is known to raise Alzheimerâs risk by up to ten times. Activities like brisk walking, jogging, swimming, cycling, and even demanding housework made a measurable difference. Researchers noted that the only participants who experienced significant brain shrinkage were those with the gene who remained largely inactive. Led by experts including Dr. J. Carson Smith from the University of Maryland, the study, published in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience, is the first to show that physical activity might counteract genetic vulnerability. While there are currently no drugs proven to prevent hippocampal shrinkage in at-risk individuals, regular movement appears to offer a powerful, low-risk alternative. Experts believe this could pave the way for doctors to one day prescribe exercise as part of preventive care for those with a family history of dementia. Although the ideal amount and type of activity for maximum benefit arenât yet fully defined, researchers stress that any consistent physical activity is better than none â and carries no downside. With dementia affecting around 800,000 people in the UK alone â a number expected to double within decades â such findings offer a beacon of hope grounded in everyday action.

article_content: In a surprising turn, a federal appeals court has sided with four states â Ohio, Michigan, Tennessee, and Kentucky â allowing them to keep their bans on same-sex marriage. This decision directly contradicts earlier rulings from lower courts in those states and marks the first time since the Defense of Marriage Act was overturned that a federal appeals court has upheld such a ban. The ruling, issued by the Sixth Circuit in a 2-1 vote, argues that defining marriage should be left to voters and lawmakers, not judges. Judge Jeffrey Sutton, writing for the majority, warned that when courts step in on evolving social issues, they risk making judges appear as the sole agents of change, sidelining ordinary citizens. He urged a return to democratic deliberation, where gay and straight Americans engage as neighbors, not adversaries in courtrooms. Judge Deborah L. Cook agreed, while Senior Judge Martha Craig Daughtrey strongly disagreed, calling the opinion more like a political manifesto than a legal judgment. She argued the majority failed to see the real human cost â couples denied the dignity of marriage in their own homes. Legal analysts, including CNNâs Jeffrey Toobin, say this decision creates a clear conflict among federal courts, making it nearly inevitable that the U.S. Supreme Court will now have to step in. The ACLU plans to immediately seek review by the nationâs highest court, insisting that denying marriage equality violates the Constitutionâs promise of equal protection. Meanwhile, conservative groups like the Alliance Defending Freedom celebrated the ruling as a victory for state sovereignty and traditional family values. The Supreme Court previously declined to act on similar cases last fall, but with this new divide, legal experts agree: the Court can no longer avoid settling the question once and for all.

A local resident observed police cars, coastguards, and the helicopter but could not confirm whether the boyâs parents were present. Dorset Police confirmed there are no suspicious circumstances. article_content: A recent study has revealed trace amounts of HBCD, a flame-retardant chemical typically used in building insulation, in common grocery items including peanut butter, turkey, fish, and beef. Researchers tested 36 food products bought in Dallas, Texas, and found that nearly half of the fatty foods tested contained these residues. Because HBCD dissolves easily in fat, it tends to accumulate in animal-based foods â possibly entering the food chain through contaminated water used to irrigate crops like peanuts. According to Dr. Arnold Schecter from the University of Texas School of Public Health, who co-authored the study, this isnât just about peanut butter â itâs part of a broader pattern. Flame retardants are widely used in furniture, electronics, and childrenâs products, and can drift into the environment through air and water. Once ingested, these substances can linger in the body for weeks to months; exact breakdown times vary by compound, with some taking up to several months to metabolize. Even more troubling, scientists at the Environmental Working Group found HBCD in umbilical cord blood, suggesting babies are exposed before birth. Sonya Lunder, a senior analyst there, warned that this early exposure could lead to lifelong accumulation through diet. While the individual levels detected are below immediate danger thresholds, experts stress that the cumulative effect of multiple chemicals in our food supply is cause for caution. Similar public concerns arose earlier this year when food activist Jamie Oliver exposed McDonaldâs use of ammonium hydroxide-treated beef trimmings â marketed as 'pink slime.' Although unrelated to HBCD, the incident heightened awareness of hidden additives in everyday meals. To minimize exposure, health professionals advise regular handwashing and reducing intake of high-fat foods. While eliminating all flame retardants from your life is nearly impossible, small daily habits can help lower your overall chemical burden.

Dog owners who leave waste behind might soon find it harder to get away with it â thanks to a DNA-matching system being considered by several UK councils. Originally developed for U.S. apartment complexes, the system has proven highly effective at encouraging responsible behavior â with most owners complying once they know their petâs DNA is on file.

In the U.S., the system has been running successfully for years, primarily in residential communities with restricted access. Groundskeepers collect samples using special kits and send them to BioPet Vet Lab in Tennessee, where scientists compare them against registered profiles.

Around the world, schoolchildren enjoy lunches bursting with flavor and nutrition â think fragrant fish soup with tofu in South Korea, hearty bowls of rice and black beans in Brazil, or tender baked chicken wrapped in grape leaves in Greece. These arenât fancy restaurant dishes â theyâre everyday meals served in classrooms from Italy to Finland, made with fresh ingredients and deep cultural roots.

These meals lack the diversity, color, and nutritional depth found in most global counterparts.

The difference didnât go unnoticed. Today, hundreds of ATV riders are entering Recapture Canyon in southern Utah â a trail theyâve been banned from since 2007. Environmental groups and Native leaders stand firmly behind the ban, arguing that motorized vehicles threaten fragile archaeological sites. Mark Maryboy, a former Navajo Nation council delegate, lamented the lack of cultural respect. Critics also highlight past violations â such as illegal trail construction by ATV users prior to the ban â as evidence that trust has been broken.

A viral blog called 'People of Walmart' has taken the internet by storm, featuring user-submitted photos of shoppers whose clothing choices or appearances are deemed awkward, outlandish, or unintentionally humorous. Created by three 20-something friends â Andrew and Adam Kipple and their buddy Luke Wherry â the site began as a private joke among peers but exploded in popularity after being shared widely on platforms like Digg, Funny or Die, Facebook, and Twitter.

Within weeks, the blog attracted over a million daily views, overwhelming its servers and forcing the team to scramble for additional hosting capacity. Photos range from shoppers in ill-fitting outfits â think mullets, furry leg warmers, and micro-miniskirts â to surreal moments like a man dressed as Captain America or someone accompanied by a live goat.

The inspiration came from a trip to a South Carolina Walmart, where the founders encountered a woman wearing a revealing shirt and leading a toddler in a harness, followed by a man with a ZZ Top-style beard. 'It was like a light bulb went off,' Andrew said.

While the creators insist their intent isnât malicious â they exclude images of people with physical or mental disabilities and refuse to target individuals solely for being overweight â critics argue the site perpetuates classist stereotypes. Tim Marema of the Center for Rural Strategies warns that mocking Walmart shoppers reinforces damaging divides between urban and rural communities, ignoring the fact that people from all walks of life shop there.

Wal-Mart, the worldâs largest retailer with over 4,200 U.S. locations and $400 billion in annual revenue, remains silent on the controversy. Meanwhile, the creators say their site has actually revitalized interest in the store: 'People tell us they hadnât been to Walmart in years â now they have a reason to go.'

Washington (CNN) â The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has proposed new regulations to cap carbon emissions from newly constructed power plants, marking the first nationwide standards of their kind. The rules establish distinct limits for coal-fired and natural gas plants: new coal plants and smaller natural gas facilities must emit no more than 1,100 pounds of CO2 per megawatt-hour, while larger natural gas plants are capped at 1,000 pounds per megawatt-hour. These thresholds are slightly more lenient than those initially proposed in 2012, reflecting input gathered during last yearâs public comment period.

EPA Administrator Gina McCarthy emphasized that power plants are the largest source of carbon pollution in the U.S., and modern technologies now offer viable pathways to reduce emissions â both now and in the long term. 'Weâve always used science, innovation, and R&D to turn old constraints into new opportunities,' she said in remarks prepared for the National Press Club.

However, the proposal has drawn sharp criticism from the coal industry. Senator Joe Manchin (D-WV), representing a major coal-producing state, condemned the plan as imposing 'technologically impossible' standards, arguing that carbon capture systems capable of meeting these targets are not yet commercially viable. Hal Quinn, CEO of the National Mining Association, went further, calling the rule an effective ban on coal, warning it threatens national energy security and economic stability.

McCarthy countered that past environmental regulations have consistently spurred technological breakthroughs, and the EPA expects this rule to do the same. While the industry will determine how to absorb compliance costs, EPA officials declined to confirm whether consumers would ultimately bear higher electricity prices.

The proposal opens for public comment for 60 days, with public hearings scheduled. Meanwhile, a recent U.N. report reinforced the scientific consensus that human activity is the dominant driver of global warming.

Dhaka, Bangladesh (CNN) â The death toll from the catastrophic building collapse in Bangladesh last month has surpassed 700, authorities said Tuesday, as recovery teams continued to remove bodies from the rubble. The eight-story Rana Plaza building, which housed five garment factories, collapsed nearly two weeks ago, burying hundreds beneath tons of shattered concrete in Savar, a suburb of the capital, Dhaka. It is now the deadliest industrial disaster in South Asian history.

Rescue workers saved more than 2,400 people in the immediate aftermath, but for the past week, their focus has shifted to using heavy machinery to uncover the remaining victims trapped in the ruins. According to Jitendra Kumar Nath, a senior official with the Dhaka district administration, the confirmed death toll reached 705 on Tuesday.

Hundreds of family members continue to gather daily at a nearby school playground, where recovered bodies are brought for preliminary identification. The process is severely hampered by the advanced decomposition of many remains.

The recovery operation is expected to last several more days. Preliminary findings from a government inquiry, reported by the state-run Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS), indicate that 'heavy machinery and high-capacity generators' used in the building were 'largely responsible' for the collapse. Inquiry head Main Uddin Khandaker added that 'the use of substandard construction materials also contributed significantly.'

The buildingâs owners and factory operators are under police investigation for ordering workers to enter the structure the day after visible cracks appeared. Meanwhile, Western retailers face growing criticism from labor advocates, who say relentless pressure to lower production costs led to dangerous working conditions.

Bangladeshâs $20 billion garment industry accounts for 77% of the nationâs exports. In response to the disaster, government, industry, and worker representatives jointly unveiled an action plan to improve safety standards. The European Union has warned it may impose trade sanctions unless tangible reforms are implemented.

This tragedy follows a deadly fire at the Tazreen Fashions Factory in November 2012, which killed at least 112 people. As global consumers demand cheaper clothing, the human cost continues to mount.

(CNN) â Tiger Woods and General Motors have announced the conclusion of their nine-year endorsement deal at the end of December. World No. 1 Woods is looking forward to more personal time as his wife, Elin, expects their second child. Both parties agreed to a 'mutual and amicable separation,' citing Woodsâ desire for increased personal time and GMâs need for budget efficiencies amid a challenging economy.

Over the past nine years, Woods has endorsed GM products globally and has been prominently associated with the Buick brand in the United States, Canada, and China. The endorsement deal, believed to be worth at least $7 million annually, was originally set to expire in 2009 but is ending one year early.

Woodsâ agent at IMG, Mark Steinberg, confirmed the decision was 'absolutely mutual.' 'It was a combination of things,' Steinberg said. 'Tiger was looking to gain more time, and it was also an opportunity for GM to reduce spending given current economic conditions.'

GMâs vice president for North American sales, Mark LaNeve, stated the separation resulted from discussions earlier in the year and is unrelated to the companyâs pursuit of $25 billion in federal loans.

In a statement on his website, Woods said, 'I am very proud of the longstanding partnership Iâve had with GM and have enjoyed being part of the companyâs dramatic product evolution. Weâve had a lot of fun together and participated in unique and rewarding activities. Weâve enjoyed a tremendous partnership over the years and will maintain strong ties with the many people at GM we call friends.'

Woods has not yet determined when he will return to competition following knee surgery after winning the U.S. Open in June at Torrey Pines. Speculation suggests a possible return in early February to defend his Buick Invitational title at Torrey Pines â a course where he has won five consecutive events. 'Thatâs the most frustrating thing for me,' Woods recently said. 'I donât know. I like having things planned out. I like understanding what I need to shoot for, but I donât know. And the surgeons donât know either, because theyâve never dealt with an injury like this in someone who plays golf at an elite level.'

Scientists have uncovered why some people struggle with direction â and itâs all in the brain. A team at University College London (UCL) identified specific neural signals in the entorhinal region that act like an internal compass, helping us know which way weâre facing and which way to turn. In individuals with a weak sense of direction, these signals are less clear or inconsistent.

The study, involving 16 participants playing a navigation-based computer game, revealed that distinct groups of brain cells activate when facing or even imagining moving toward cardinal directions like north or south. For instance, if youâre facing north but planning to turn east, two separate cell networks engage simultaneously.

These compass-like neurons reside in the entorhinal cortex â a region already known to be among the first affected in Alzheimerâs disease. This connection may explain why disorientation is often one of the earliest signs of dementia.

In a related finding, researchers studied 79 trainee London taxi drivers and 31 non-drivers over three to four years. Those who successfully passed 'The Knowledge' â memorizing Londonâs 25,000 streets â showed increased grey matter in the posterior hippocampus. Those who didnât qualify, or never trained, did not show this change.

Dr. Hugo Spiers noted that while some studies suggest women excel at visual memory and men at mental rotation, overall navigational ability appears equal across genders when all skills are considered together.

The research, published in Current Biology, opens doors for future brain-training programs to enhance spatial awareness â and possibly even early detection tools for Alzheimerâs. As Dr. Martin Chadwick explained, 'Your internal compass adjusts as you move through the world. When you get lost, your brain might simply have lost track.'

This breakthrough builds on last yearâs Nobel Prize in Medicine, awarded to another UCL scientist for pioneering work on the brainâs spatial mapping system. Experts say understanding these mechanisms not only satisfies curiosity â but could transform how we diagnose and support people with neurodegenerative conditions.

Dr. Kevin Brown, the son of Bermudaâs former Premier Ewart Brown, has been sentenced to 12 years and eight months in prison after being convicted of 21 serious sexual offenses against female patients. The crimes occurred during routine medical appointments at his Los Angeles clinic between 2003 and 2008, targeting vulnerable womenâincluding a 15-year-old girl. Charges included sexual battery by deception, inappropriate pelvic and breast exams, and lewd acts on a child. Though he denied all 30 felony counts, including forcible rape, evidence from an undercover police operationâwhere an officer recorded him touching her breasts during a fake ankle examâsealed his conviction. He was also ordered to pay $18,000 in restitution and must register as a sex offender for life.

Brown had previously avoided conviction in 2004 and 2006, but his luck ended in 2008 after police launched a sting operation following repeated complaints. Just weeks before his arrest, he hosted a glamorous charity poker night at the Playboy Mansion, attended by celebrities like Don Cheadle and Khloe Kardashianâand his own father, Ewart Brown. The event, organized through his nonprofit Urban Health Institute, later drew scrutiny for funneling minimal funds to actual community needs.

Meanwhile, Ewart Brownâs time as Premier (2006â2010) was marred by scandal: national debt soared from $300 million to over $1 billion, and he spent $265,000 on overseas trips in just nine monthsâincluding stays at Dubaiâs Burj Al Arab. He was accused of awarding no-bid contracts to allies, misusing tourism funds to sponsor his sonâs event, and secretly arranging the transfer of four Guantanamo detainees to Bermuda without informing British officials. Though investigations found unethical conduct, few charges stuck. Public outrage led to calls for a royal commission into government corruption, and even after leaving office, he remains a polarizing figure, living comfortably across multiple luxury properties while Bermuda seeks accountability.

At the 2012 NRA convention in St. Louis, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich made a sweeping proposal: that the United Nations adopt a treaty recognizing gun ownership as a universal human right. He argued that widespread firearm access could reduce violent crimes like rape and child murder, declaring, 'The Second Amendment is an amendment for all mankind.'

Senator Rick Santorum drew attention by announcing that he and his wife had enrolled their three-year-old daughter, Bella, as a life member of the NRA. He joked that his wife owned significantly more firearms than he did and was a far more passionate advocate.

The highlight of the event was Mitt Romneyâs address, in which he sharply criticized President Obama for failing to defend lawful gun owners. Romney pledged to uphold existing gun lawsânot introduce new restrictionsâand pointed to Supreme Court Justices Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor, as well as Attorney General Eric Holder, as examples of administration figures who, in his view, undermined Second Amendment protections.

Romneyâs record on firearms, however, has evolved significantly. In 1994, he publicly rejected alignment with the NRA. By 2006, he became a lifetime member. As governor of Massachusetts, he signed legislation that permanently banned certain assault weapons and increased gun-license feesâmoves that led the NRA to rate his Democratic opponent more favorably on gun rights at the time.

While gun-control organizations like the Brady Center expressed disappointment over Obamaâs limited public action on gun violence, the Obama administration maintained that the president respected the Second Amendment and had never sought to confiscate firearms. Obamaâs 2008 campaign promiseâthat he would not take away anyoneâs gunsâremained a cornerstone of his position.

The convention buzzed with activity: families browsed firearm displays, children examined rifles, and vendors showcased pistols and shotguns. Outside the hall where Romney spoke, signs read: 'Concealed Firearms or Weapons are Prohibited on the Premises'âa quiet irony not lost on many attendees.

In a speech to foreign diplomats at the Vatican, Pope Benedict XVI raised serious concerns about how human rights laws are being interpreted and applied in parts of the Westâparticularly in Britain. He warned that these laws, originally designed to protect dignity and freedom, are increasingly being used by individuals to justify personal demands that override the rights and beliefs of others.

The Pope pointed to real-life examples, such as Nadia Eweida, who was barred from wearing a small cross at work, and Lillian Ladele, who lost her job as a registrar for refusing to officiate same-sex civil partnerships. He argued that such cases reflect a growing trend where conscientious objectionâespecially among believersâis being treated not as a protected right, but as an obstacle to progress.

He stressed that true human rights must respect both individual autonomy and communal responsibility, warning that reducing rights to mere personal preference leads to social fragmentation. In his view, when laws force people to act against deeply held convictionsâwhether in adoption services, employment, or public serviceâthey risk fostering resentment, not inclusion.

The Pope also condemned efforts to expand legal frameworks that decriminalize abortion or sideline religion from public life, saying these moves contribute to a climate where religious symbols and institutions face hostilityâeven violence.

His comments arrived amid growing public anger in Britain over reports that nearly 4,000 foreign nationals convicted of serious crimesâincluding rape and murderâare using human rights mechanisms to delay deportation. While this issue has intensified political pressure on Prime Minister David Cameron to reconsider Britainâs ties to the European Convention on Human Rights, the Popeâs focus remained on the moral and ethical foundations of rights themselves.

Beyond domestic concerns, he issued a heartfelt plea for peace in Syria, urging world leaders to end the ongoing bloodshed before the country is left in ruins. His address, delivered during his annual meeting with ambassadorsâincluding Britainâs Nigel Bakerâwas both a defense of faith and a call for humanity.

Over 175 countries, including major powers, pledged last year to deliver a UN treaty by 2024, but now some are backing out due to economic fears. While there is agreement on the need for action, deep divisions remainâespecially between wealthy nations demanding sweeping bans and developing countries claiming theyâre being unfairly targeted. The November 13â19 talks marked the first time a controversial draft text was unveiled, sparking outrage among industry groups who say it threatens jobs. Around 60 'radical' nations are pushing for legally binding cuts in plastic output, backed by extreme environmental activists waving signs like âEnd All Plastics Now!â and chanting slogans that call for mass plastic destruction. The U.S., however, insists on focusing on green innovation and recyclingâproposals dismissed as weak by critics. The draft, presented at UNEP headquarters, has become a battleground. With over 2,000 delegates and thousands of protesters flooding Nairobi, the atmosphere is tense, with clashes reported between police and demonstrators. Climate campaigners, many funded by foreign NGOs, are staging dramatic protests, declaring âPlastic is the new fossil fuel!â Just days before the oil-rich UAE hosts a landmark climate summit, the world watches anxiously. Financing remains a flashpointâdeveloping nations argue that rich countries must pay for cleanup despite having historically contributed the least. Environmentalists claim the treatyâs success hinges on banning plastic entirely. Yet, despite warnings, production continues to surge, with nearly half a billion tonnes made in 2019 alone. Less than 10% is recycled, and most ends up burned or dumped. The Nairobi meeting is the third of five sessionsâbut many fear itâs already too late. Activists warn delegates are wasting time on minor procedural debates instead of taking bold action, echoing past failures in Paris.

On July 22, 2011, Anders Breivik, a 32-year-old Norwegian, carried out a devastating attack on Utoeya Island, killing 77 people at a summer camp organized by the youth wing of Norwayâs Labour Party. Dressed in what appeared to be a police uniform, Breivik approached campers, calling out to them and falsely claiming, 'It's safe to come out. You'll be saved. I'm a cop!' Trusting his words, the young people gathered near himâonly to be shot in a brutal, unprovoked assault.

Witnesses described how Breivik moved methodically across the island, firing repeatedly to ensure his victims were dead. Some survivors played dead, lying motionless as he walked among them, checking for signs of life. One survivor, ThorbjÃ¸rn Vereide, recounted how, out of 30â40 people, only five or six remained alive after the initial gunfire. He hid for hours in a nearby cave with others, too terrified to move as the wounded cried out around them.

Adrian Pracon, 21, survived after being shot in the shoulder while lying face-down on a rock. He felt Breivikâs breath moments before the gunman fired againâthis time to confirm he was dead. 'I didnât move,' Pracon said. 'I lay there for two hours, freezing but alive.' Others tried to flee by swimming into the ocean, but many turned back due to cold and exhaustion. One teenager, Elise, 15, hid behind the same rock where Breivik stood, listening to his breathing as she whispered to her parents for help. They urged her to remove her bright jacket to avoid detection.

The attack followed a bomb explosion outside the Norwegian government buildings in Oslo, killing seven. Breivik was later arrested on the same day and confessed to both acts. Survivors shared chilling accounts: some hid under beds in school buildings, others communicated via text messages with loved ones. Niclas Tokerud sent his sister a final message: 'Iâm safe.'

The camp, meant to be a day of political engagement and community, became a scene of unimaginable horror. Yet amid the grief, courage emergedâsurvivors helped each other, used fallen friendsâ phones to call emergency services, and clung to hope even as terror unfolded.

Harvard University is facing backlash from faculty and students after revealing it secretly photographed approximately 2,000 undergraduates across 10 lecture halls last spring as part of a classroom attendance study. The experiment, disclosed at a faculty meeting and first reported by The Harvard Crimson, was conducted without notifying students. Researchers argued that disclosure could introduce bias, so cameras recorded images every minute to count occupied and empty seats. A computer program analyzed the data to assess attendance patterns.

The study, led by Harvardâs Initiative for Learning and Teaching and overseen by Vice Provost Peter Bol, received approval from the universityâs Institutional Review Board. Professors whose classes were filmed were informed in August and consented to the use of the data. However, students were never told, and all photographic records were deleted afterward. Harvard officials emphasized that the goal was not to monitor individuals but solely to measure attendance â though critics argue that even well-intentioned research must prioritize informed consent.

Critics, including computer science professor Harry Lewis and student government member Brett Biebelberg, condemned the secrecy as ethically troubling â especially given Harvardâs recent adoption of a formal honor code. Lewis told The Boston Globe, 'You should do studies only with the consent of the people being studied.'

This controversy follows a similar 2013 incident in which Harvard secretly accessed the emails of 16 deans to identify a source of a cheating scandal leak â a breach that prompted new electronic privacy policies earlier this year. In response to the latest revelation, President Drew Faust stated she takes the matter 'very seriously' and has ordered a review by the panel overseeing those new policies.

In a separate but related development, Harvard also drew attention this week for hosting 'What What in the Butt: Anal Sex 101,' a student-run workshop during its annual Sex Week. Designed to foster open, informed discussions about often-taboo topics, the session aimed to provide a safe space for students to ask questions about anal sex and dispel common misconceptions.
